The results provided in this paper contribute to a deeper understanding of the practicality of wave induced VIV harvesting, highlighting some potential challenges associated with deploying such a system.

articleTitle: Design and Optimization of Wing Shape for Underwater Glider Based on CFD
abstract: The wings of the underwater gliders (UGs) are the main physical feature that distinguishes them from other underwater robots. Optimization of wing parameters based on computational fluid dynamics (CFD) is one of the important ways to improve its gliding performance. This paper proposed an optimization method of wing based on the orthogonal method and the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm by considering the drag coefficient, lift-to-drag ratio, and moment coefficient (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${{\bm{l}}_{\bm{\alpha }}}$</tex>) as optimize objectives, which are closely related to the range of UGs. After the optimization of the wing parameters, the drag coefficient was reduced by 47.30 %, the lift-to-drag ratio was augmented by 36.71 %, and the la was diminished by 79.32 % at an angle of attack of 6 ° and a flow velocity of 0.5 m/s. The above cases prove the effectiveness of the optimization method proposed in this paper, which can find the best solution among a large number of wing parameters and reduce the need for large data samples and high computing power in CFD simulation.

articleTitle: Variational Mode Decomposition-Based Self-Noise Cancellation in Oceanic Environment
abstract: This research addresses the persistent challenge of self-noise in towed arrays of SONAR ships, which often hinders the detection of faint targets due to their higher energy levels. We propose a novel self-noise cancellation (SNC) method employing a variational mode decomposition to overcome this issue. The approach involves decomposing the noisy data, comprising clean and noise components, into intrinsic mode functions (IMFs). The noisy data is initially subjected to variational mode decomposition to extract its underlying IMFs. These IMFs represent different signal frequency components. Subsequently, we assess the cor-relation coefficient between the IMFs of the noisy data and the undesired signal. An appropriate threshold is then applied to selectively eliminate the self-noise components, preserving the essential signal information. To validate the effectiveness of our method, we present experimental results using beam patterns, waterfall displays, and output signal-to-interference-noise ratios (SINR). The beam patterns showcase the directional sensitivity of the towed array, emphasizing the reduction in self-noise interference. Waterfall displays offer a temporal perspective, illustrating the improved clarity of target signals over time. Output SINR is the difference between power at target and self-noise bearing (in dB) after SNC.

articleTitle: On Line Identification Method of Roll Center Deviation for Underwater Glider
abstract: The center of gravity of the underwater glider is not absolutely located in its longitudinal plane even well-trimmed, with the biofouling in the long-term deployment, the lateral deviation of the center of gravity may gradually expand resulting side slip and yaw motion. In addition, the lateral disturbance of random ocean currents will also make yaw controller oscillate repeatedly. Intense oscillation amplitude will affect the navigation stability and the sampling quality of the sensor. This paper first analyzes the reasons for yaw motion oscillation and proposes the roll center deviation compensation method to solve this problem. Secondly, based on the approximate linear relationship between the roll rudder angle and the yaw angular velocity obtained by the data from simulation and sea trail, an on-line identification method of the roll center deviation is proposed. Finally, through a long-term sea trial, the feasibility and stability of this method are verified, besides, a quantitative evaluation was conducted on the energy conservation effect promoted by this method.

articleTitle: An Improved IMMENS Framework to Handle Conflicting Temporal Plans in mAritime Environments
abstract: The IMMENS framework focuses on enabling the dynamic cooperation of a collection of maritime on-board cyber-physical systems to collectively plan towards an overall (global) goal. In this paper we propose to augment the original IMMENS framework with a new module that implements a formal approach from the literature to facilitate the handling of temporal conflicts in plans. To show that the module is able to handle a sufficiently complex fusion of sub-plans to be incorporated into IMMENS, we applied it to a use-case taking inspiration from the literature. This use-case was used to show that the new module facilitates the merging of sub-plans with temporal dependencies by combining all events in the sub-plans, recalculating the temporal dependencies and finding possible incoherence in the final plan and pointing out where conflicts arise. We present the module and motivate its benefits. With this feature, IMMENS can temporally merge sub-plans. Furthermore, the new module can provide assistance to solve incoherent plans, which was an issue during temporal fusion before.

articleTitle: Dynamically Feasible, Collision-Free Trajectories for Autonomous Marine Surface Vehicles
abstract: Kinodynamic path planning involves generating paths that respect the differential system constraints. Such paths are especially important for ASVs, as holonomic paths are not always achievable. The Rapidly Exploring Random Tree (RRT) is a well known algorithm for kinodynamic path planning. An RRT is used to forward integrate the system dynamics for several ASV models, propagating them forward in time, to produce a list of control inputs that transition each system from its start state to its goal state. In this paper, computational benchmarks are shown for four ASV models, and kinodynamic plans for each model are demonstrated. The authors present the respective outlooks of for each model, discussing the work as a method of re-planning with regards to collision detection and avoidance. The result show a fast sub-optimal planner for the production of valid dynamically feasible ASV paths, suitable for a priori motion planning.

articleTitle: URoBench: Comparative Analyses of Underwater Robotics Simulators from Reinforcement Learning Perspective
abstract: In an effort to standardise the evaluation of Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms across different simulators of underwater robots, this paper introduces a benchmark framework, URoBench, to test the capabilities of simulators in RL- related tasks of underwater robotics. This framework is characterised by its modular architecture. By abstracting these components, the framework allows for integration with various simulators through different interfaces. To verify the framework, we tested the performance of three typical underwater robotics simulators (HoloOcean, Dave, and Stonefish) in RL conditions. Also, the usage effectiveness of the computation resources of these three simulators was compared. The verification result demonstrates the feasibility of incorporating this benchmarking framework into different simulators, facilitating consistent and comparable assessments. This benchmarking framework stands to provide a common assessment method for underwater robot simulators, standardising the development and simulation of RL for marine robotics.

articleTitle: Generalized Approach for Modeling and Control of Structurally Variable Underwater Vehicles
abstract: The paper presents a generalized approach for modeling and control of structurally variable underwater vehicles. For this purpose, an iterative and automatable design loop consisting of eight steps has been developed as framework. The first four steps deal with vehicle module assembly and dynamic modeling of the resulting mission vehicle. The hydrodynamics of the vehicle shape are predicted and lead to the parameterized nonlinear differential equation of motion in six degrees of freedom. The other steps are related to the control system design to satisfy the mission plan, which serves as input for the design framework. For designing the control system, the necessary operation modes are defined, required actuator allocations are calculated and a holistic control system is parameterized, where dedicated controllers are used in a structurally modular control system to map the modularity of the mission dependent operations. Finally, a verification of the designed control system and the estimation of the system performance is realized, with focus on feasibility of the planned mission. The paper concludes with exemplary simulations using the design framework as comparison to experimental trials using a functional model of a defined vehicle configuration.

articleTitle: Flight Dynamics of an Underwater Glider with Passively Adapting Flapping Wings
abstract: This paper examines the flight dynamics of an underwater glider using a passive flapping-foil glide concept. Therefore an analytical description of the gliding path, based on the acting hydrostatic and hydrodynamic forces is introduced. Afterwards, a study based on computational fluid dynamics for various flow cover geometries is conducted. Based on the simulations a suitable flow cover is selected. Lastly the chosen geometry is fabricated as a model and examined in wind tunnel tests. Based on the experimentally determined force coefficients and the before introduced theoretical relationships, the system's gliding movement can finally be calculated and statements regarding glide efficiency are made. The results are compared to the conventional glide concept used in today's legacy gliders and are discussed.

articleTitle: Linear Time Complexity Algorithms for Time Domain Simulations of the Structural Mechanical Behaviour of Submarine Power Cables in Offshore Wind Power Applications
abstract: A part of modern submarine power cables is freely suspended in the water column and subject to hydrodynamic loads. It is thus important to carry out time domain simulations of design load cases as a basis for the investigation of the cables' mechanical fatigue behaviour. Accordingly, numerically performant models are required to simulate a large variety of metocean- and loading conditions. In consequence, different numerically efficient models are derived within the context of this paper and compared regarding their performance and accuracy.

articleTitle: Acknowledgement Strategies for the JANUS Medium Access Control Protocol
abstract: The JANUS protocol, as the first standardized underwater communication protocol, aims to become the reference means of communication between underwater devices. For compatibility and ease of implementation, its initial Medium Access Control (MAC) layer specification is left as plain as possible. In this paper, we present an extension of the JANUS protocol involving data packet acknowledgments (ACKs) and retransmissions to improve the reliability of underwater acoustic networks (UAN) powered by this protocol. This extension will enable more complex applications with back-and-forth messaging or usage of the protocol in more challenging acoustic environments. As part of this work, an initial Logical Link Control (LLC) module and three different ACK integration strategies are proposed that produce the following three JANUS Link Layer protocol variants: JANUS-ACK, JANUS-Quick-ACK (JANUS-QACK), and JANUS-Interrupt-ACK (JANUS-IACK). These three variants of the JANUS protocol enhance it by integrating the ACK functionality at the Link Layer. In this work, we implement and simulate these protocols in multiple scenarios with a range of different parameters to provide a general overview of their comparative performance, as well as comparing them with ALOHA and Time Division Multiple Access (TDMA) benchmark protocols. JANUS-QACK and JANUS-IACK show promising results with up to a 50% throughput improvement compared to JANUS-ACK, and provide a good trade-off amongst throughput, latency and number of re-transmissions required for successful delivery compared with ALOHA and TDMA.

articleTitle: Adaptive Model Predictive Control with Online System Identification for an Unmanned Underwater Vehicle
abstract: Unmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs) are increasingly important for various underwater tasks, and achieving autonomy for UUV s is a major focus. This is crucial for enhancing safety, flexibility, extending operational range, and reducing costs. However, designing effective and robust control algorithms for UUV s is challenging due to nonlinear dynamics, uncertainties, constraints, and environmental disturbances. Model predictive control (MPC) is a well-established technique for UUV control, while how to obtain accurate prediction models becomes the key challenge for improving controller performance. This paper proposes an online system identification method based on an extended active observer (EAOB) and the recursive least squares with variable forgetting factor (RLS- VFF) algorithm to estimate environmental disturbances and identify uncertain hydrodynamic parameters. The estimated disturbances and parameters are continuously updated in the MPC's prediction model to generate optimal control inputs based on the real-time environment and vehicle conditions. The proposed approach is validated through the Gazebo and robot operating system (ROS) simulation environment, demonstrating its effectiveness in handling uncertainties and disturbances for UUV control.

articleTitle: Development of High Accuracy CTD Sensor: 5EL-CTD
abstract: The authors have developed a new CTD sensor with the primary objective of achieving high accuracy to address the requirements for analyzing the impacts of global warming. The conductivity sensing cell is based on the five electrode principle. The temperature sensor consists of a thermistor with a diameter of 0.43 millimeters. For the pressure sensor, a reliable OEM product has been utilized. Additionally a calibration bath capable of sea water and demonstrating temperature stability within a range 0.0005 degrees Celsius over ninety seconds, was developed. The C- and T-sensor underwent primary calibration with the assistance of JAMSTEC, Japan. T-sensor successfully achieved a combined uncertainty of less than 0.001 degrees Celsius. However, the C-sensor yielded incomplete results, with a preliminary estimate of its uncertainty at approximately 0.002 mS/cm. The depth sensor, calibrated using a dead weight tester maintains its uncertainty within 0.1 percent full-scale range. A subsequent calibration procedure to bridge the primary to secondary step, facilitated by a soaking block, was explored. The result indicated satisfactory performance in temperature calibration but many rooms for improvement in that of conductivity. Finally, a field test was conducted at the coast of Japan, producing promising results for CTD profiling. The developed sensor demonstrates potential in contributing to accurate and reliable data collection for assessing the effects of global warming.

articleTitle: Multi-View 3D Reconstruction of Vessel Hull with Spatial Density Weighted NeRF
abstract: A bstract- The 3D reconstruction of vessel hulls is crucial for enhancing safety, efficiency, and knowledge in the maritime industry. Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) is an alternative for 3D reconstruction and rendering from multi-view images, particularly tensor-based methods have proven effective in improving efficiency. However, existing tensor-based methods typically suffer from a lack of spatial coherence, resulting in gaps in the reconstruction of fine-grained geometric structures. This paper proposes a spatial density weighted NeRF (DW-N eRF) for accurate and efficient surface reconstruction of vessel hulls. The proposed method develops a weighted feature space decomposition mechanism, which utilizes tensorial radiance fields and weighted algorithms to extract feature vectors of sampled points. To enhance training efficiency, a coarse-fine strategy is employed for the density-weighted algorithm during the training process. Extensive experiments conducted on a synthetic vessel hull (SVH) dataset demonstrate that the effectiveness of our method in achieving remarkable rendering quality, high reconstruction accuracy and timeliness.

articleTitle: Development and Sea Trials of the Wenhai-1 Hybrid Underwater Vehicle for Comprehensive Survey of Gravity, Magnetism, Topography, and Sampling
abstract: Deep-sea autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) play a crucial role in marine exploration but are limited primarily to sensor data collection and seafloor mapping. Recognizing the need for exploration, inspection, and intervention tasks, there is a growing interest in hybrid underwater vehicles. These vehicles, powered by self-contained batteries and equipped with manipulators, offer autonomous navigation, exploration, and intervention capabilities. This paper introduces Wenhai-l, a new hybrid deep-sea vehicle developed at the Shenyang Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Wenhai-l operates in various modes and is equipped with oceanographic survey devices, manipulators, and sensors. Sea trials in the South China Sea validated its design, highlighting the effective integration of detection and intervention tasks. Wenhai-l has demonstrated potential applications in environmental studies, oceanography, geology, and biology, positioning itself as a versatile platform for comprehensive underwater operations.

articleTitle: Integrating a Digital Twin Concept in the Zero Emission Sea Transporter (ZEST) Project for Sustainable Maritime Transport Using Stonefish Simulator
abstract: In response to stringent emission reduction targets imposed by the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and the European Green Deal's Fit for 55 legislation package, the maritime industry has shifted its focus towards decarbonization. While significant attention has been placed on vessels exceeding 5,000 gross tons (GT), emissions from coastal and short sea shipping, amounting to approximately 13% of global shipping transportation and 15% within the European Union (EU), have not received adequate consideration. This abstract introduces the Zero Emission Sea Transporter (ZEST) project, designed to address this issue by developing a zero-emissions multi-purpose catamaran for short sea routes, shown in Figure 1.

articleTitle: Vulnerable Marine Ecosystems Survey Pilot Missions with EVA Hybrid AUV/ROV
abstract: Fishing for deep-sea species occurs on continental slopes, ridges, and seamounts. Fishing operations using fishing gears that contact the bottom (e.g., trawls and bottom longlines) may have significant impacts on Vulnerable Marine Ecosystems (VMEs). VMEs refer to marine ecosystems with a population or community of sensitive taxa or habitats that are likely to experience substantial alteration from short-term to chronic disturbance and that are unlikely to recover during the timeframe in which the disturbance occurs. The VME concept, introduced in the United Nations General Assembly Resolution 61/105, has been worldwide applied to the management of deep-sea fisheries. However, the effective identification and management of VMEs is highly constrained by the scarcity of data on VME indicator taxa. This data deficiency is usually surpassed by the use of VME predictive modelling. Video footage is a non-destructive method commonly used for exploring and investigating areas of seabed and for characterising and identifying habitat types. Remotely Operated Vehicles (ROVs) are one of the tools for seabed mapping. ROVs range in size from small observation-class to large work-class vehicles. Their sizes determine the payload, manoeuvrability, depth rating and ultimately uses of the vehicle. For epifaunal imaging, ROVs can be used in two modes: qualitative inspections and quantitative assessments. This paper presents the development of an innovative system composed of a compact support research vessel and a hybrid autonomous underwater vehicle capable of accurate georeferenced high-resolution imaging and profiling of the seabed for a detailed survey of the seabed for biodiversity studies. The experimental results obtained by the developed system in field work in real VME survey at 600m depth are presented.

articleTitle: Experimental Assessment of Miniature Wave-Energy-Converter Performance: Output Analysis in Simulated Wave Conditions
abstract: This paper presents an experimental performance assessment of a Miniature Wave Energy Converter (MWEC) in simulated wave conditions. The MWEC is designed to harvest small amounts of energy from ocean waves for a potential application as a Zero-Power-Wakeup mechanism for sensor activation. The study investigates the MWEC's output characteristics under diverse movement conditions, including both harmonic and non-harmonic motions. To achieve this, a methodology for characterising performance in a controlled laboratory environment using a hexapod is implemented. The study provides valuable insights in alternative testing methods of Wave Energy Converters (WEC). Preliminary testing results demonstrate the potential applicability of the MWEC and underscore the need for rigorous testing methodologies in the development and evaluation of WEC.

articleTitle: Sonar SLAM in Structured Underwater Environments
abstract: Underwater environments pose a challenge to Si-multaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) performed by autonomous underwater vehicles (AUV), as underwater struc-tures are typically featureless with few references of motion. In turbid waters, sonar sensors must be used instead of cameras and LiDARs due to the properties of the water medium. A complete framework for underwater sonar SLAM in two dimen-sions is presented, built as a graph-based SLAM with submap registration. The keyframes of the SLAM are submaps of the surroundings, generated from a subset of the most recent frames. Keyframes are incrementally registered and two loop closure strategies are employed to correct the accumulated drift: one based on visual feature matching and bag-of-words, and the other based on refining the point cloud alignment of nearby keyframes. A robust pose graph optimization globally optimizes the path of the robot and the map of the environment, discarding loop closure outliers. The proposed pipeline is evaluated through real-world data collected from a marina underwater environment.

articleTitle: Forward-looking Sonar Based Autonomous Aquaculture Inspection
abstract: In recent years, there has been a rising interest in aquaculture development due to the increasing demand for food driven by population's growth. Aquaculture infrastructures require regular monitoring to assure their preservation and food safety, traditionally conducted by slow and risky manual methods involving professional divers. To solve this issue, an autonomous aquaculture net inspection using an Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV) is proposed. The AUV is equipped with a Forward-Looking Sonar (FLS), which provides acoustic images of the environment. By using image processing techniques to remove noise, the vehicle's distance and orientation relative to the net cage are measured. The net cage's center is estimated, using a circle regression, to compute the relative orientation. Then, velocity and orientation references are generated, so the AUV can cover the net whole perimeter, while staying at a desired distance. Finally, many tests are performed to analyze the vehicle's behavior while encircling the net.

articleTitle: A Preliminary Study on Spectral Unmixing for Marine Plastic Debris Surveying
abstract: We present a pilot study where spectral unmixing is applied to hyperspectral images captured in a controlled environment with a threefold purpose in mind: validation of our experimental setup, of the data processing pipeline, and of the usage of spectral unmixing algorithms for the aforementioned research avenue. Results from this study show that classical techniques such as VCA and FCLS can be used to distinguish between plastic and nonplastic materials, but struggle significantly to distinguish between spectrally similar plastics, even in the presence of multiple pure pixels.

articleTitle: SPEC: Simulating Acoustic Scattering for Wide Aperture Sparse Array Multibeam Receivers
abstract: A future deep-ocean bathymetry sensor could be developed from a swarm of disconnected, distributed receivers attached to Autonomous Surface Vehicles (ASVs) forming a very wide aperture multi-beam array. This system would be able to collect high-resolution readings at depths beyond traditional systems. Novel processing techniques must be developed to analyze the data collected by such a system, however to evaluate these algorithms, precisely localized ground-truth data must be available, which is currently not feasible to collect. Additionally, a swarm-based system is capable of reconfiguring its layout to optimize the data collection, however evaluating such a swarm controller requires rapid collection of data. This paper discusses efforts to synthesize the time series data needed for these use cases. Several acoustic simulation tools are evaluated for synthesizing backscatter and bi-static reflection data collected at arbitrary surface positions for multiple detector array and sea floor configurations. In addition, a purpose built solution, Scattered Pressure Echo Capture (SPEC), is described and compared with the established modeling tools. SPEC is able to generate time series data for all examined seafloor configurations, however the other tools are unable to model the deep configuration. In order to provide a reasonable comparison, a scaled version of the problem is developed based on a physical configuration reported in the literature. The tools are used to synthesize receiver data for the scaled version. Near-field beamforming is performed, focusing the receivers at the known bathymetry, and no additional processing is performed. The results are evaluated based on the in-phase signal producing an amplitude spike sufficient for predicting the true bathymetry. Error metrics are presented for each tool including SPEC. In addition, the results for the deep water configurations for which only SPEC was able to handle are given. None of the examined tools generated data from which perfect predications could be made, however this synthesized time series data may be adequate for evaluating future algorithms developed to process the data collected by a swarm-based wide aperture sea floor imaging system.

articleTitle: Estimating the Diffuse Downwelling Attenuation Coefficient from in Situ Photographs
abstract: The rate at which water absorbs and scatters light in the vertical direction is governed by the diffuse downwelling attenuation coefficient. Despite having some dependence on environmental conditions, the diffuse downwelling attenuation coefficient is strongly influenced by water constituents, making it useful for optically characterizing water bodies, assessing water quality, or quantifying visibility. Here, we present a simple method with which the spectral diffuse downwelling attenuation coefficient can be estimated from in situ photographs of a color target, taken by an ordinary camera. This estimation is achieved through optimization contingent upon knowing the following: 1) the reflectance spectra of the color target patches, 2) the spectral response of the camera, and 3) the depths at which the photos are taken. We present results from nine locations in the northern Red Sea, which reasonably match ground truth values obtained using a commercial underwater radiometer. Our method utilizes low-cost parts that can be set up to be lowered from a boat, or carried by a diver. Data processing needs little computational resources, and in principle, the system can be configured as a real-time tool for monitoring pollution, blooms, climate change effects, etc., especially in coastal areas where ocean color data from satellites may be unavailable or operating profiling instruments may be logistically challenging. The resulting data can also be useful for validating satellite-derived estimates, where available, or supporting underwater computer vision applications.

articleTitle: Power Demand Forecasting for a Hybrid Marine Energy System with Shallow and Deep Learning
abstract: To ensure that future autonomous surface ships sail in the most sustainable way, it is crucial to optimize the per-formance of the Energy and Power Management (EPM) system. However, marine EPM systems are complex and often coordinate various distributed energy resources, energy storage systems, and power grids to ensure reliable and safe power delivery. Traditional control methods for marine EPM systems are limited by evaluating processes using simplified component models over a short time horizon, or relying on historical insights gained from earlier journeys, and are not the optimal approach for complex hybrid marine EPM systems. Advanced control strategies, such as Model Predictive Control (MPC), offer a promising control method that considers predicted future system responses over an extended time horizon to determine the best control input, making them an effective strategy for optimizing the performance of hybrid marine EPM systems. However, to learn the onboard energy profiles based on component behavior in a hybrid system from past experiences is not a trivial task, and one of the primary barriers to implementing MPC for marine EPM control. For this reason, in this work, we address the challenge of learning energy profiles for a marine EPM system by utilizing shallow and deep machine learning for total power demand forecasting. The forecast is an essential reference for an MPC-based controller and will enable this control strategy to provide reliable and safe power delivery for hybrid marine EPM systems. The proposed approach compares state-of-the-art machine learning models to identify the best-performing algorithm, considering accuracy and computational requirements. We illustrate the potential of the proposed approach by using real world operational data from a vessel with a hybrid marine EPM system. Results indicate that shallow models, trained on engineered features handcrafted with classical signal processing techniques, allow forecasting the total power demand up to a horizon of 5min with minimal loss in accuracy and a negligible computational burden.

articleTitle: Acoustic Metasurfaces-Assisted High-Data-Rate Underwater Communication with Ocean Dynamics
abstract: Acoustic metasurfaces (AMS) are ultra-thin meta-materials of sub-wavelength thickness, which are known for their non-conventional manipulation of sound waves. In this work, we study fundamental limits when an AMS is employed in dynamic underwater acoustic communication systems. In terms of channel capacity, we show that an AMS-assisted link outperforms the conventional single-link communication and achieves high data-rates over long ranges. We establish that the physical placement of AMS near either transmitter or receiver maximizes the received signal-to-noise-ratio. Further, we show that by choosing large enough number of meta-atoms, the AMS-assisted link outperforms a decode-and-forward relay network, in terms of capacity. For our simulations, we use BELLHOP ray-tracing software to obtain the beam information, and then incorporate the Hall-Novarini bubble cloud model, VirTEX platform motion and VirTEX sea surface motion algorithms to take ocean dynamics into consideration. Thus, utility of AMS paves the way for long-range underwater communication with enhanced data-rates.

Author Keywords: VirTEX sea surface motion and platform motion models

articleTitle: Online Informative Sampling Using Semantic Features in Underwater Environments
abstract: The underwater world remains largely unexplored, with Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) playing a crucial role in sub-sea explorations. However, continuous monitoring of underwater environments using AUV s can generate a sig-nificant amount of data. In addition, sending live data feed from an underwater environment requires dedicated on-board data storage options for AUV s which can hinder requirements of other higher priority tasks. Informative sampling techniques offer a solution by condensing observations. In this paper, we present a semantically-aware online informative sampling (ON- IS) approach which samples an AUV's visual experience in real- time. Specifically, we obtain visual features from a fine-tuned object detection model to align the sampling outcomes with the desired semantic information. Our contributions are (a) a novel Semantic Online Informative Sampling (SON-IS) algorithm, (b) a user study to validate the proposed approach and (c) a novel evaluation metric to score our proposed algorithm with respect to the suggested samples by human subjects.

articleTitle: Cooperative Control of AUVs for Obstacle Avoidance Under Trajectory
abstract: This research presents a novel approach for implementing cooperative control for obstacle avoidance in Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) through the utilization of sonar technology for obstacle detection and position determination. The study establishes a motion model for AUVs and designs an interactive topology structure based on position information using Sonar systems. By integrating sonar-based position detection, the study develops a cooperative control method that enables AUV clusters to achieve coordination and collision avoidance based solely on position information. The proposed method facilitates the coordination of clusters, obstacle avoidance, and task execution, effectively resolving conflicts among these elements while ensuring the maintenance of a safe distance. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through the successful control of AUV clusters along a specific trajectory, showcasing its capability in achieving cluster coordination and obstacle avoidance.

articleTitle: Understanding the Mechanism and Variability of Chlorophyll a Concentration in the Waters Surrounding the Philippines
abstract: Phytoplankton plays a crucial role in marine life as it is the primary producer in food webs, providing energy for higher trophic levels. Understanding the seasonal variation of chlorophyll-a concentration in the Philippines can provide valuable information about the distribution patterns of phytoplankton. In this study, we aimed to comprehend the mechanism and variability of chlorophyll-a concentration in the waters surrounding the Philippines, including its seasonal changes, and how meteorological variables (such as sea surface temperature, rainfall, and wind) and oceanic circulations (such as Ekman Transport, Ocean Current, and ENSO) contribute to its variability. The results of this study showed that coastal waters generally have higher chl-a concentration, while open seas have lower chl-a concentration. Additionally, the highest seasonal chl-a concentration is found during the winter season (DJF) with the presence of an offshore chl-a patch in the north-western Philippine Sea (WPS). Conversely, seasonal chl-a concentration is at its lowest during spring (MAM). About 33% of the total chlorophyll-a variability showed a direct covariation in all seasons between the West Philippine Sea and the Philippine Sea that occurs every six years during winter and spring seasons, and every nine years during summer and autumn seasons. The concentration of chlorophyll-a is influenced by meteorological variables such as wind, rainfall, and sea surface temperature. Along the coasts, stronger winds and increasing rainfall result in higher chlorophyll-a concentration, while weaker winds and decreasing rainfall lead to lower concentration. Ekman Transport showed a direct relationship to chlorophyll-a in some parts of WPS and an inverse relationship in the northern West Philippine Sea wherein stronger (weaker) offshore Ekman Transport results in higher (lower) chlorophyll-a concentration. The El Niño Southern Oscillation has varying effects on the chlorophyll-a concentration across the seas of the Philippines. Lastly, the Kuroshio Current (KC) has a significant impact on the oceanic conditions in the western North Pacific.

articleTitle: An Improved Underwater Target Detection Algorithm Based on YOLOX
abstract: Aiming at the problem that the accuracy of underwater target detection algorithms is poor due to the complex marine environment, a target detection network algorithm that can quickly detect four types of marine organisms is proposed, which is improved based on YOLOX. Firstly, the Double-pair CLAHE-Gamma multi-scale image processing is carried out through the marine images to alleviate the blurring effect of image degradation caused by the marine environment, which facilitates the subsequent detection task. Secondly, the SimAM attention mechanism and GhostMode are introduced to improve the original backbone CSPDarkNet, which improves the representation capability of the network while preserving the target features. Then, inspired by the RFB feature model, the feature network RFB-liteSimAM is proposed to replace the backbone feature extraction network SPPBottleneck, to improve the size of the sensory field region. Finally, the advantages of image high-level features and bottom-level features are combined by introducing two weighted eigenfeatures that increase the feature propagation ability at different levels and improve the detection accuracy. The experiments show that the improved algorithm achieves a mAP of 81.13% compared to YOLOX-s, which is an improvement of 3.59%. Compared with YOLO-m, the mAP is improved by 0.88%, the model size is reduced by 66.24%, and the FLOPs are reduced by 65.20%. The algorithm is helpful to be applied to the navigator for the real-time detection of marine organisms, which can provide a reference for the detection of other marine targets.

articleTitle: The optimal tracking control for Autonomous Underwater Vehicles Using ESO and MPC algorithms
abstract: Considering the complexity and uncertainty of the marine environment and the unknown underwater environmental disturbances and rudder angle saturation constraints during the control and tracking process, a control algorithm based on an extended state observer (ESO) combined with model predictive control (MPC) is proposed. Firstly, based on the dynamic characteristics of the AUV, its dynamic model is established, and the AUV plane motion equation and vertical plane equation are obtained by simplification. Secondly, the extended state observer is used to estimate external disturbances, and the model predictive control is used to explicitly handle the rudder angle saturation constraint. The minimization of rudder angle switching and tracking error is taken as the optimization objective. Finally, the control effect is compared with that of widely used classical PID algorithm by simulation experiment. The comparison results show that the proposed algorithm can improve path following effect.

articleTitle: Robotic Data Recovery from Seabed with Optical High-Bandwidth Communication from a Deep-Sea Lander
abstract: This paper addresses the problem of high-bandwidth communication and data recovery from deep-sea semi-permanent robotic landers. These vehicles are suitable for long-term monitoring of underwater activities and to support the operation of other robotic assets in Operation & Maintenance (O&M) of offshore renewables. Limitations of current commu-nication solutions underwater deny the immediate transmission of the collected data to the surface, which is alternatively stored locally inside each lander. Therefore, data recovery often implies the interruption of the designated tasks so that the vehicle can return to the surface and transmit the collected data. Resorting to a short-range and high-bandwidth optical link, an alternative underwater strategy for flexible data exchange is presented. It involves the usage of an AUV satellite approaching each underwater node until an optical communication channel is established. At this point, high-bandwidth communication with the remote lander becomes available, offering the possibility to perform a variety of operations, including the download of previously recorded information, the visualisation of video streams from the lander on-board cameras, or even performing remote motion control of the lander. All these three operations were tested and validated with the experimental setup reported here. The experiments were performed in the Atlantic Ocean, at Setúbal underwater canyon, reaching the operation depth of 350m meters. Two autonomous robotic platforms were used in the experiments, namely the TURTLE3 lander and the EVA Hybrid Autonomous Underwater Vehicle. Since EVA kept a tether fibre optic connection to the Mar Profundo support vessel, it was possible to establish a full communication chain between a land-based control centre and the remote underwater nodes.

articleTitle: Underwater MEMS Gyrocompassing: A Virtual Testing Ground
abstract: In underwater navigation, accurate heading in-formation is crucial for accurately and continuously tracking trajectories, especially during extended missions beneath the waves. In order to determine the initial heading, a gyrocom-passing procedure must be employed. As unmanned underwater vehicles (UUV) are susceptible to ocean currents and other disturbances, the model-based gyrocompassing procedure may experience degraded performance. To cope with such situations, this paper introduces a dedicated learning framework aimed at mitigating environmental effects and offering precise underwater gyrocompassing. Through the analysis of the dynamic UUV signature obtained from inertial measurements, our proposed framework learns to refine disturbed signals, enabling a focused examination of the earth's rotation rate vector. Leveraging recent machine learning advancements, empirical simulations assess the framework's adaptability to challenging underwater conditions. Ultimately, its contribution lies in providing a resilient gyrocompassing solution for UUVs.

articleTitle: Novel Approach for Offshore Photovoltaic Panels Inspection with VTOL UAV
abstract: Solar energy will contribute to global economic growth, increasing worldwide photovoltaic (PV) solar energy production. More recently, one of the outstanding energy achievements of the last decade has been the development of floating photovoltaic panels. These panels differ from conventional (ter-restrial) panels because they occupy space in a more environmen-tally friendly way, i.e., aquatic areas. In contrast, land areas are saved for other applications, such as construction or agriculture. Developing autonomous inspection systems using unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV s) represents a significant step forward in solar PV technology. Given the frequently remote and difficult-to-access locations, traditional inspection methods are no longer practical or suitable. Responding to these challenges, an in-novative inspection framework was developed to autonomously inspect photovoltaic plants (offshore) with a Vertical Takeoff and Landing (VTOL) UAV. This work explores two different methods of autonomous aerial inspection, each adapted to specific scenarios, thus increasing the adaptability of the inspection process. During the flight, the aerial images are evaluated in real-time for the autonomous detection of the photovoltaic modules and the detection of possible faults. This mechanism is crucial for making decisions and taking immediate corrective action. An offshore simulation environment was developed to validate the implemented system.

articleTitle: Overview and Performance Assessment of Different Multicarrier Waveforms for Wideband Underwater Acoustic Communication
abstract: Underwater Acoustic communication channels are usually characterized by their time-variant nature and undergo frequency-selective fading. Additionally, the signaling bandwidth of underwater acoustic communication often represents a significant proportion of the center frequency, effectively making underwater acoustic communication wideband, particularly for moderate and high data rate communications. In wideband underwater channels, the Doppler effect induces a non-uniform, frequency-dependent shift of signal frequencies throughout the bandwidth. Our work focuses on some emerging multicarrier modulation schemes, namely Orthogonal Delay-Scale Space Modulation(ODSSM), Orthogonal Delay-Doppler Division Multiplexing(ODDM), Orthogonal Time Sequency Multiplexing(OTSM), and Orthogonal Chirp-Division Multiplexing(OCDM), which shown superior performance over the widely recognized OFDM in highly doubly spread channels. This work provides a detailed overview of these potential multicarrier modulation schemes. Additionally, we examine the effectiveness of these emerging multicarrier modulation schemes found in current literature, utilizing a low-complexity equalizer, over underwater acoustic communications characterized as wideband, highly time-varying, and highly frequency-selective. Numerical simulations clearly demonstrate that all the con-sidered modulation schemes, such as ODSSM, ODDM, OTSM, and OCDM, outperform the commonly used method, Orthog-onal Frequency Division Multiplexing(OFDM) across wideband underwater acoustic channels. Notably, the ODSSM modulation technique surpasses the overall performance of all considered modulation waveforms.

articleTitle: Towards Efficient Underwater Robotic Swarms: Edge-Based Comparative Analysis of Multi-Object Trackers
abstract: This article conducts a comparative analysis of State-Of- The-Art (SOTA) multi-object trackers, focusing on their performance when tracking homogeneous swarms of robots and their suitability for edge device deployment. The comparative analysis can serve as a valuable tool for assessing the viability of employing different detectors and Multi-Object Tracking (MOT) models in developing autonomous underwater robotic swarms that can be utilized in various applications such as search and rescue, seabed scanning, environmental monitoring, etc. The evaluation centers around two real-time SOTA multi-object trackers, namely ByteTrack and OCSort, both operating on the tracking-by-detection (TBD) paradigm. Additionally, detectors such as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathbf{YOLOv5n}, \mathbf{YOLOv8n}$</tex>, and YOLOXn are considered. The study employs two distinct MOT datasets, DanceTrack and BrackishMOT, for assessing accuracy metrics such as ROTA, MOTA, and IDF1 as well as latency. The findings offer practical insights into the optimal combination of detectors and MOT models, crucial for enhancing the efficiency and performance of autonomous underwater robotic swarms. This research serves as a valuable reference for researchers and practitioners in the field, providing a foundation for the development of advanced systems capable of addressing diverse challenges in underwater environments.

articleTitle: Passive Multi-Sensor Fusion for Tracking Underwater Targets: Field Experience from REPMUS22
abstract: Robotic Networks equipped with passive sensors, which can detect the noise emitted by targets moving in the ocean, represent a covert and effective solution for the surveillance of large underwater areas. In this context, advanced information fusion methodologies, which are able to coherently fuse the generated bearing-only measurements and track existing underwater targets, are required to achieve a comprehensive underwater survelliance capability in anti-submarine warfare (ASW) scenarios. This paper will focus on the performance of the delta-generalized labelled multi-Bernoulli <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(\delta-\mathbf{GLMB})$</tex> tracking filter, an information fusion methodology which was employed during the Robotics Experimentation and Prototyping MUS (REPMUS22) and Dynamic Messenger (DYMS22) trials, held in Portugal in September 2022. In particular, we will show that the 6-GLMB tracking filter is able to effectively fuse passive measurements generated by a hybrid robotic network composed of two bottom sensing nodes and two autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), thus enabling near real-time monitoring of large underwater areas.

articleTitle: Self-Prior Guided Diffusion Model for Marine Snow Removal
abstract: Underwater images are commonly subject to diverse degradation factors in the intricate underwater environment, which impedes the application of computer vision underwater. Marine Snow, as a prevalent degradation factor of underwater images, poses significant challenges for marine snow removal due to its complexity (e.g., varying sizes and shapes). However, existing marine snow removal approaches oversimplify the complexity of marine snow particles, and the bottom-up removal methods overlook the background blur and fogging effects caused by these particles, resulting in blurred details in the restored image. Motivated by the recent advancements in diffusion-based generative models, we propose a self-prior guided diffusion model (SPGDiff) for effective marine snow removal. Specifically, we first obtain the self-prior information by developing a global understanding of complex marine snow particles. Subsequently, the self-prior information is incorporated into the diffusion model. Guided by the self-prior information and leveraging its strong generative capability, the diffusion model progressively recovers image details, so that the generated image finally obtains high-resolution texture and high-fidelity details. We conduct extensive experiments on public datasets of marine snow, including MSRB and Snowy-VAROS, demonstrating the exceptional performance of our method for marine snow removal.

articleTitle: Optimization Strategies for Sail Angles of Unmanned Sailboats based on CFD and VPP
abstract: This paper focuses on the optimization strategies of sail angles in unmanned sailboats under various wind conditions. CFD and VPP are employed to conduct an in-depth analysis of unmanned sailboat performance. By comparing the CFD simulations with VPP calculations, the paper highlights the necessity of precise sail angle adjustment in real sailing conditions and points out the discrepancies between theoretical models and practical applications. The paper also discusses future research directions, including further optimization of simulation models, incorporation of more environmental factors and real sailing conditions, and conducting actual sailing trials to validate and improve theoretical models.

articleTitle: Quantized Model-Parameter-Free Tracking Control for Autonomous Underwater Vehicles with Dead-Zone Nonlinearity
abstract: This paper investigates the issue of model-parameter-free trajectory tracking control for autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) considering input quantization and unknown dead-zone nonlinear dynamics. Firstly, a totally model- parameter- free architecture with sliding mode control is exploited to force the tracking errors converging to a residual set, which implies that the proposal will possess desirable robustness to parameter variations. Then, in order to effectively decrease the communication rate from control module to the actuators, a hysteresis quantizer is applied to produce piece-wise quantized control signals. Parameters of this quantizer are integrated into the control scheme such that tracking accuracy is rarely sensitive to quantization errors. Thereafter, external disturbances and input dead-zone dynamics are tackled via adaptive laws. Finally, theoretical analysis indicates that the position and orientation errors can be uniformly ultimately bounded. And numerical simulation results are provided to illustrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed controller.

articleTitle: Evaluating the Performance of Internal and External Modulator for Underwater Visible Light Communication System
abstract: In the research area of underwater wireless communication systems, our study is mainly focused on enhancing the performance of Underwater Visible Light Communication (UVLC) systems, especially in conditions typified by weak oceanic turbulence, absorption, and scattering phenomena. This emphasis resulted from the realization that turbulence in underwater environments frequently occurs in variable degrees and has a direct impact on UVLC performance. We use the log-normal distribution as a statistical model to describe the behavior of fading coefficients in order to address the difficulties brought on by weak oceanic turbulence. These coefficients, which are crucial factors in determining the operation of UVLC systems, are vulnerable to statistical variations under settings of light ocean turbulence. Our main objective is to improve UVLC system performance, and to do this, we evaluate the performance of UVLC system using internal and external modulators. Enhancing the dependability and effectiveness of UVLC systems working in areas with weak oceanic turbulence requires these performance evaluations. To accomplish this, we thoroughly investigate the effects of these factors on critical performance indicators as the bit-error rate (BER), Q-factor, and communication range. These parameters are essential for figuring out how well UVLC works overall for underwater communication. Our method combines meticulous simulations with empirical research to produce insights that can guide UVLC system configuration decisions. Our goal is to improve the robustness and effectiveness of UVLC system in difficult underwater conditions by deploying different types of modulators in the UVLC system.

articleTitle: Mission Planning and Safety Assessment for Pipeline Inspection Using Autonomous Underwater Vehicles: A Framework Based on Behavior Trees
abstract: The recent advance in autonomous underwater robotics facilitates autonomous inspection tasks of offshore infrastructure. However, current inspection missions rely on predefined plans created offline, hampering the flexibility and autonomy of the inspection vehicle and the mission's success in case of unexpected events. In this work, we address these challenges by proposing a framework encompassing the modeling and verification of mission plans through Behav-ior Trees (BTs). This framework leverages the modularity of BTs to model onboard reactive behaviors, thus enabling autonomous plan executions, and uses Beha Verify to verify the mission's safety. Moreover, as a use case of this framework, we present a novel AI -enabled algorithm that aims for efficient, autonomous pipeline camera data collection. In a simulated environment, we demonstrate the framework's application to our proposed pipeline inspection algorithm. Our framework marks a significant step forward in the field of autonomous underwater robotics, promising to enhance the safety and success of underwater missions in practical, real-world application https://github.com/remaro-network/pipe_inspection_mission.

articleTitle: Improved ICM-DDQN Obstacle Avoidance Method for Unmanned Underwater Vehicle
abstract: Autonomous obstacle avoidance is a key technology for unmanned underwater vehicle (UUV) to perform autonomous navigation and autonomous operations. In this paper, the Intrinsic Curiosity Module Double Deep Q network (ICM-DDQN) algorithm is proposed to study the end-to-end UUV path planning of discrete action output. To improve the ability of the autonomous obstacle avoidance algorithm to explore and learn optimal navigation and obstacle avoidance policy in an environment without a map and with sparse rewards, the internal reward of the curiosity module is introduced as a reward enhancement signal. Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) are used to capture the correlation of long-distance features and extract dynamic features so that the prediction error in the feature space of the intrinsic curiosity module provides a good intrinsic reward signal. In addition, to improve the stability and efficiency of ICM-DDQN network training, a dynamic compound reward is designed to guide the UUV to the target. Both simulation and experimental results show that this algorithm improves the reward value and accelerates the convergence speed, allowing UUV to obtain the optimal path in a complex unknown environment.

articleTitle: Exploring Feature Modalities with Cross Attention Network for the Detection of Remotely Operated Underwater Vehicles
abstract: Detection of underwater Remotely Operated Vehicles (ROVs) is vital due to security concerns associated with their potential use for covert purposes. The distinct acoustic signature of ROVs generated by their electric motor set them apart from other underwater acoustic sources. These acoustic signatures are the extracted acoustic features from the self-recorded ROV audio signals (self-curated dataset) that determine the performance of the detection system. While many temporal and spectro-temporal features struggle to capture these acoustic characteristics independently, we propose a fusion of features in a cross-attention framework called the Bi-Modal Cross-Attention Network (BiMCAN). This network investigates the interplay between the two features employed for detecting ROVs. We specifically focus on exploring Wavelet Scattering Transform (WST) as one feature for its noise resilience, variation stability, data efficiency, and integration capabilities within a model. For the other feature, we delve into temporal and spectro-temporal features for ROV detection. Our evaluation of the BiMCAN covers accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score and includes a comparison with other models regarding trainable parameters.

articleTitle: Free-Rising Microstructure Profiler in Full-Water-Column of Ocean
abstract: Turbulent mixing within a few meters near the ocean surface and bottom plays a crucial role in air-sea and sea-solid interactions, but it is often under-sampled due to observational challenges. To address this issue, the Free-rising Full-water-column Microstructure Profiler (FFMP) has been developed to perform the microstructure measurement in full water depth under an undisturbed condition. FFMP has a spherical shape and possesses the advantages of low fluid resistance, minimal disturbance, and easy operation. The main sensor package on FFMP includes fast-response thermistors (FP07), conductivity-temperature-depth (CTD), acoustic trans-ducer, three-dimensional (3D) inclinometer, and acceleration. In the in-situ application, the FFMP attached with a disposable iron anchor is deployed from the ship deck downwelling to the sea floor. After making sure that the FFMP arrives on the sea floor, the acoustic signal from the ship is sent to release it by dropping off the anchor. The FFMP rises freely through the whole water column, meanwhile, the full-water-column microstructure signals are recorded. Turbulent dissipation rate is inferred based on the theoretical spectral analysis of the microstructure data. On the sea surface, the FFMP transmits radio signals to facilitate location for recovery. The FFMP has been tested in the South China Sea with the water depth ranging from 28 to 3095 m, and the results are verified to be consistent with those of the commercial free-falling microstructure profiler.

articleTitle: SeaTecHub: Croatia-Cyprus Excellence Hub on Eco-Innovative Technologies for Healthy and Productive Seas
abstract: Blue Economy represents an important economic source in Croatia and Cyprus with around 10% of jobs in each country being related to Blue Economy. Thinking on this fact, the main goal of the SeaTecHub project is to strengthen Croatian and Cyprus place-based innovation ecosystems and improve access to excellence for R&I actors by cross-border collaboration on a common strategy and alongside value adding chains within the area of eco-innovative technologies for healthy and productive seas, focusing on sectors 1. Aquaculture and fisheries, 2. Smart ports, 3. Maritime security and protection, 4. Research and Education, and 5. Maritime technologies. To do so a set of measures including joint strategy, action and investment plans, joint R&I projects and knowledge exchange activities is being implemented. This paper reports on the initial project work related to the joint strategy and other activities during the first months of the project.

articleTitle: The JANUS Underwater Communications Standard: From Promulgation to Present
abstract: JANUS is a NATO standard (STANAG 4748) [1] and is the first internationally adopted digital underwater acoustic communications standard. In a nutshell, it is a simple and robust modulation and coding scheme that can be easily adopted by a wide range of existing systems. JANUS has been developed by the NATO STO Centre for Maritime Research and Experimentation (CMRE), in collaboration with Academia and Industry, with the goal to break the interoperability barrier of digital underwater acoustic systems. JANUS technical specification is available without security markings from the NATO standardization Office (NSO). Therefore, it is open and free for use by military and civilian operators. As of 2024, JANUS is still the only open standard for digital underwater acoustic communications. This document describes the evolution of JANUS from its promulgation on March 24th 2017 to present. It covers some of the JANUS milestones regarding the engagement with the operational community and Industry, definition of applications and scenarios, at-sea experimentation, up to the most recent STANAG revision.

articleTitle: Wave Induced Vibration Energy Harvesting
abstract: Ocean waves hold great promise as a renewable energy source, yet effectively harnessing this energy necessitates the enhancements of technologies. Despite the advancements in Wave Energy Converters (WECs), several current limitations in wave energy harvesting technologies hinder widespread commercial adoption. WECs have demonstrated their potential for electrical power generation but there is a recognition that a single type of energy harvesting mechanism may not fully exploit the vast energy potential of the marine environment. This study explores Vortex Induced Vibrations (VIV) as a complementary energy har-vesting mechanism for WECs: the basic idea is to exploit wave-induced VIV. The paper investigates the viability of this approach, focusing on clarifying the necessary conditions required to enable this innovative energy harvesting approach. The results provided in this paper contribute to a deeper understanding of the practicality of wave induced VIV harvesting, highlighting some potential challenges associated with deploying such a system.

articleTitle: Sparse Representation of the Acoustic Ocean Impulse Response for Real-Time Simulation of Sonar Reverberation
abstract: Acoustic reverberation from the ocean surface and seafloor is a dominant source of non-stationary noise and false alarms in low frequency active sonar operations. The numerical simulation of this phenomenon is computationally expensive when relying on the usual technique of summing the reverberant contributions from all points of a fine mesh of ocean boundaries. This computational burden is particularly critical when the Doppler spread of the signals has to be calculated. The average energetic envelope of the reverberation formally reduces to a pair of 2D integrals of functions over the surface and bottom; these functions include the acoustic impulse responses (IR) between the sonar and the points over the ocean boundaries. The usual technique relies on evaluating the properties of eigenvalues connecting the sonar and all the points forming a fine grid. In this paper, we present a more compact method based on a sparse representation of the IR over a coarse sampling of the ocean boundaries. This faster technique describes the impulse response from an elemental scatterer sampling the surface, as a function of time using only six parameters: the total intensity, the means and standard deviations of the delays and grazing angles at the bottom and surface, and the cross-correlation between the delays and grazing angles. These parameters vary more slowly than the detailed features of the eigenvalues and can therefore be sampled over a coarse mesh, statistically with no loss of information. The evaluations of the integrals to be estimated are then faster, allowing real-time evaluation of the reverberation. We demonstrate the validity of our method by comparing the reconstructed impulse responses and reverberation levels with the full solution, and by replicating the environmental conditions of a previous sea-trial with strong seabed anistropy. The results indicate an acceptable level of similarity between the two approaches, while the new method enables simulation of complex seabed reverberation with a significant gain in computational efficiency.

articleTitle: Development and Demonstration Experiments of the HAMADORI Seaplane UAV
abstract: Continuous and efficient ocean monitoring is vital for environmental, disaster, and maritime security. Traditional methods like manned ships are costly and offer limited observation, while unmanned alternatives face mobility and access challenges. The HAMADORI series, including the HAMADORI3000 and HAMADORI6000, aims to overcome these issues. The HAMADORI3000, designed for aerial surveillance with a 3-meter wingspan and electric propulsion, targets a 2-hour flight duration and 20m/s speed. The more versatile HAMADORI6000, with a 6-meter wingspan and engine systems, can carry various payloads and cover the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). It features GNSS-A technology for geodetic observations and a hydrophone for underwater acoustics, demonstrating the feasibility of advanced marine research techniques. Additions like a winch system for deploying sensors highlight its potential for diverse applications. Ultimately, the HAMADORI UAVs offer innovative, cost-effective solutions for comprehensive maritime monitoring, with the HAMADORI6000's versatility opening new avenues for marine research and conservation.

articleTitle: The Design of a Global Oceanic Plastic Debris Monitoring System Using Imaging Spectroscopy Onboard Low-Flying Satellites
abstract: The distribution and behavior of the vast accumulation of plastic waste in the oceans, often referred to as the ‘plastic soup’, are heavily influenced by plastic debris coming from rivers and coastal areas. Currently, the location and dynamics of the oceanic ‘plastic soup’ is already well understood. However, the exact process behind the formation of this plastic soup remains incompletely comprehended. This knowledge gap can be linked, in part, to the absence of worldwide detailed spatiotemporal data collected from ground and space. This is specifically due to the lack of detection and imaging techniques with a high spatial and temporal resolution. To address this gap, an innovative concept is proposed based on imaging spectroscopy. The goal is to address and further improve the observed spectral signatures of different plastics by imaging the observed scenery. In order to distinguish between these different kinds of plastics, a dedicated optical filtering system with a high resolution and revisit time has to be designed. Therefore, the concept is based on an Acousto-Optic Tunable Filter (AOTF), specifically designed for remote sensing and imaging. In order to achieve a high temporal resolution, being able to capture the evolution and movement of plastic in the oceans, a constellation of satellites are foreseen. Therefore, a low flying platform and deployable optics are introduced. Flying at 300 km altitude instead of a typical > 600 km for Earth observation satellites, reduces the required imaging aperture.

articleTitle: Informative path planning in complex marine environments: Gap imputation and variance minimization in satellite data
abstract: Satellite remote sensing plays a critical role in operational oceanography by providing Near Real Time (NRT) measurements of essential climate variables (ECVs), such as Sea Surface Temperature (SST) and Salinity with extensive spatial coverage compared with in-situ measurements. However, these parameters are obtained through passive measurements with satellite data that often suffer from attenuation due to atmospheric effects, resulting in missing data in satellite recordings. To overcome this issue, we propose a novel approach towards intelligent autonomous measurement acquisition that outlines the potential use of Unmanned Surface Vehicles (USVs). The aim is to measure at locations with missing data by combining information-driven exploration and energy-efficient path planning. Information-driven exploration refers to identifying potential measurement points with high informativeness. We use differential entropy as information metric based on a Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) model that uncovers the variances in the satellite data. Subsequently, we plan a path of an USV by extending the Rapidly-exploring Random Tree Star (RRT<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">*</sup>) algorithm by introducing an energy-dependent cost function considering Sea Surface Currents (SSC) to accurately capture the complex marine environment. By this, we introduce a modified information metric trading out informativeness and energy consumption in the path planning. The results demonstrate that informative and energy-efficient path planning can significantly reduce the USV’s energy consumption, with potential savings of up to 88%.

articleTitle: The Pareto Optimal Evasion Strategies in Reach-Avoid Differential Games Between Heterogeneous UUVs
abstract: This paper considers a reach-avoid differential game between heterogeneous UUVs in a rectangular play region, and a set of Pareto optimal evasion strategies is given. The evader aims to reach the target line without being captured, while the pursuers strive to prevent that by capturing the evader. The evader has a minimum turning radius. We focus on constructing a barrier in the time domain for this variation of differential games under great rigorous circumstances in which the opponent possesses great maneuverability and complete information perception ability. First, the restriction of the differential game proposed in this paper is given. Second, the Trajectory-Tree planning method with continuous state action is given, and the decision-making mechanism of both sides is explained. We build a mechanism for modifying UUV's rationality, and the problem of barrier construction is transformed into multi-objective optimization. Then, a variation of the multi-objective optimization algorithm is presented to acquire the Pareto evasion strategy set. Finally, the effectiveness of the algorithm has been verified in a confrontation with multi-pursuers.

articleTitle: A Wirelessly-Enabled, Power-Optimized, Low-Cost, and Open-Source Durafet-based pH Instrument for Continuous, Long Term Environmental Monitoring
abstract: The increasing acidity of our oceans, exacerbated by human activities, represents a growing threat to the human societies that rely upon healthy marine ecosystems. Research activities to collect data on the progression of ocean acidification are a crucial part of efforts to monitor, assess, and mitigate impacts. However, high-cost, commercially available monitoring tools represent a major barrier to comprehensive data collection and community engagement, especially for ocean acidification research. Here, we present an iteration to our open-source, low-cost pH sensor design which utilizes a Durafet pH electrode. We developed significant improvements to optimize energy consumption, simplify assembly, and add wireless functionality while maintaining affordability. We performed low-power hardware and firmware modifications which extend the battery lifespan. We designed a custom PCB that reduces assembly error, improves modularity, and maintains a compact footprint. Finally, we implemented bi-directional wireless functionality in our design, enabling wireless data retrieval and sensor re-programming, a feature that is notably absent in commercially available counterparts. With the addition of these features, we have designed open-source pH sensor electronics that are more affordable and accessible while maintaining high performance. Expanding sensor networks benefits everyone, by equipping researchers, policymakers, and communities with the knowledge and resources required to understand and adapt to our rapidly changing world.

articleTitle: Learning Seabed Properties and Sensitivities from Ship Noise Spectrograms
abstract: In this work, deep neural networks are trained on synthetic spectrograms of transiting ships to find properties of the seafloor and uncertainty labels associated with those predictions. The spectrograms are labeled with the values of sediment layer thickness, sound speed, density, and attenuation; and a measure of the parameter information content or sensitivity for each parameter obtained from the Cramér-Rao bound (CRB). The CRB values for a given ocean environment and source-receiver geometry can be calculated and expressed as a relative uncertainty, for each sediment property. To obtain uncertainty labels for each spectrogram, the relative CRB is calculated for ten equally spaced frequencies for each sediment parameter of interest. These relative CRB values are divided into uncertainty classes, and the mode class across frequency is assigned as the uncertainty label for the spectrogram. The labeled synthetic spectrograms are used to train ResNet-18 networks, which can then tested on measured spectrograms. Comparisons are made between validation performance of networks that are trained to learn only the parameter value labels and those trained to learn both seabed parameter values and sensitivity class. The validation results indicate the potential to predict not only sediment properties but uncertainty in those predictions.

articleTitle: A Channel-estimation-aided Underwater Acoustic Localization Method in the Integrated Communication and Positioning System
abstract: Underwater localization is critical for in the marine exploration. However, the harsh underwater conditions, like the multipath effect, signal attenuation and Doppler effect, introduces numerous difficulties for the underwater localization. In this paper, we propose a channel-estimation-aided underwater acoustic localization method in the underwater acoustic integrated communication and positioning (UWA-ICP) system. In the UWA-ICP system, a UWA-ICP device with a four-element hydrophone array and a transducer is equipped on each underwater node for acoustic positioning and communication. In order to mitigate the influence of multipath effect on the localization performance, an enhanced orthogonal matching pursuit algorithm is presented to perform the channel estimation. The estimated channel impulse response is used to compensate the received signal in order to mitigate the multipath effect. Numerical results show that the proposed localization method can effectively improve the localization performance.

articleTitle: Underwater Sound Source Range Estimation Based on Deep Learning
abstract: The underwater sound source ranging method based on deep learning (DL) is studied in this paper. Unlike the traditional matched field processing (MFP) method, the DL method does not require accurate environmental parameters to generate copy fields and can complete the range estimation in the absence of environmental parameters. In this paper, different deep network models are selected to complete the task of sound source ranging. Convolutional neural networks (CNN) are good at extracting local features but need more layers and parameters to capture global information, which will lead to problems such as model overcrowding. Transformer can model the whole situation on a large scale but cannot capture local features. Combining convolution operation with self-attention mechanism, a proper model based on CNN and Transformer is proposed to estimate the distance of underwater sound sources, proving effective enough by the sea trial data. Experimental results show that, CNN combined with the Transformer model has the best performance compared with Feedforward Neural Network (FNN) and CNN methods under different bandwidth and depth of sound sources.

articleTitle: Impact of River Inputs on Sound Speed Structures in the Bay of Bengal
abstract: The Bay of Bengal (BoB) exhibits a distinctive pattern of surface freshening primarily resulting from runoff originating from several major rivers and the monsoon precipitation. This freshening significantly modulates the spatial and temporal variations in the thermohaline structure, ultimately shaping the sound speed structure within this region. This study investigates the seasonal impact of river input on the sound speed structure of the BoB through two numerical simulations with and without river input using the Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS). The findings indicate that river inputs consistently reduce the surface sound speed across the domain throughout the year, with the most noticeable effect occurring in the northern part of BoB during the post-monsoon months of October and November. During this period, the surface variability is predominately driven by salinity variations induced by river inputs. In contrast, in the subsurface layers, the influence of reduced salinity becomes less pronounced with increasing depth, and the temperature modulations brought about by river inputs play a more important role. Freshening in the surface layers leads to the creation of a stratified barrier layer just below the mixed layer. Consequently, this results in the formation of warm temperature inversions in the subsurface layers, with cooling occurring beneath them. These phenomena contribute to variations in the sound speed, causing it to increase within the inversion layer and decrease below it. Notably, the sonic layer depth (SLD) is found to become shallower in the presence of river inputs during the post-monsoon and winter seasons in the northern BoB. The combination of enhanced vertical salinity gradients and subsurface temperature inversions significantly amplifies the vertical gradient of sound speed above the SLD. This, in turn, may lead to the development of more robust surface ducts and the expansion of shadow zones beneath the SLD.

articleTitle: Hybrid ROV/AUV underwater robotic system for safe and robust remote operations
abstract: Over the past years, the class of Hybrid Remotely Operated Vehicles (HROVs) has emerged as a groundbreaking innovation in marine robotics, by combining the advantages of Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV) and Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) technologies. These vehicles are designed for deep-sea exploration and intervention, capable of transitioning between different operational modes to perform a variety of underwater tasks within a single cruise deployment. This work focuses on the development of a highly versatile HROV with four distinct operational modes, determined by the level of autonomy and the presence or absence of the cable.
